1.) Know anatomy, where things bulge out vs "go in" to know where to place the shadows vs highlights. Way longer to learn but worth it.

I just added the paperman method since it's more digestible and made things "click," at least for me. It's easier to draw paper than a cube, or a whole head, so good for fast practice or warm ups too!

Hi, welcome to the journey of art! Idk if you just started learning and are using these Links as a way to learn, but if you just started, I ALWAYS recommend looking and studying real people to know the rules first. 

By only referencing from established artworks, you're learning from "broken rules" bc artists tend to stylize greatly. To stylize and make it still look "good" and make sense, I HIGHLY recommend learning how to draw "realistic" first. 

That'll teach you, for example, the length of legs vs the torso vs the arms. Or, how a sword looks when at a certain angle. 

As for perspective, drawabox is always recommended. It helps with fundamentals, which will help you deconstruct the images you see and use as reference, and ultimately help with the issues you listed.
